# Experimental Session Protocol

**Study:** A Comparative Analysis of Code Quality Generated by ChatGPT (GPT-4o),
Claude (3.5 Sonnet), and GitHub Copilot Using Software Engineering Metrics

**Version:** 1.0  
**Authors:** Syakira Putri Zahara, Raphael Aditya Isworo, Nikita Ananda Putri Masaling  
**Supervisor:** Edy Irwansyah

---

## Purpose

This document records the exact procedural constraints followed during data
collection. It is intended to enable replication by third-party researchers
and to provide a written audit trail for peer review.

All procedures described here were **finalized and locked before any code
generation session began** on 2025-04-01.

---

## 1. Pre-Experiment Locking Procedure

Prior to opening any AI interface:

1. All 10 task prompts were drafted, reviewed, and saved to `data/tasks.json`.
2. All unit test suites were written and saved to `tests/test_cases.py`.
3. The manual readability rubric was finalized and saved to `rubric/readability_rubric.md`.
4. Both raters independently confirmed understanding of the rubric criteria.
5. The evaluation pipeline `scripts/evaluate.py` was written and validated
   on a dummy dataset before any real outputs were collected.

**No prompt, test case, or rubric criterion was modified after code generation began.**

---

## 2. Model Access Configuration

### 2.1 ChatGPT (GPT-4o)

- **Interface:** OpenAI web interface — https://chat.openai.com
- **Model:** GPT-4o (confirmed in the model selector dropdown)
- **Session policy:** A new conversation was started for each of the 10 tasks.
  The browser tab was closed and reopened between tasks to prevent cross-task
  context carryover via conversation history.
- **Custom instructions:** Disabled for the duration of the experiment.
- **Login account:** Dedicated research account (not shared with personal use).

### 2.2 Claude (3.5 Sonnet)

- **Interface:** Anthropic web interface — https://claude.ai
- **Model:** Claude 3.5 Sonnet (confirmed in the model selector)
- **Session policy:** Each task was submitted in a new conversation. Existing
  conversation threads were not reused.
- **Projects feature:** Not used; all sessions were started from the standard
  new-conversation entry point to prevent persistent instructions.

### 2.3 GitHub Copilot

> **Critical control decision:** GitHub Copilot was accessed exclusively through
> the **Copilot Chat panel** in Visual Studio Code (v1.89.1), not through inline
> suggestion mode.

**Rationale:** Copilot's inline suggestion mechanism responds to the content of
open files in the active editor, making prompt equivalence across models
impossible if inline mode is used. Submitting the same natural-language prompt
through Copilot Chat provides the closest operational equivalent to the
single-turn conversational interface used by ChatGPT and Claude.

**Configuration:**
- VS Code version: 1.89.1
- GitHub Copilot extension: v1.200.0
- **Fresh VS Code window for each task:** A new VS Code window was opened
  with no workspace folder and no files open in any editor tab.
- Copilot Chat panel opened via `Ctrl+Shift+I`.
- The prompt was pasted into the chat input and submitted with Enter.
- **Inline suggestion (ghost text) was disabled** via
  `"editor.inlineSuggest.enabled": false` in VS Code settings for the
  duration of the experiment.

---

## 3. Prompt Submission Procedure

For each of the 10 tasks, the following procedure was followed identically
for all three models:

1. Copy the `standardized_prompt` field from `data/tasks.json` for the
   current task.
2. Open a new session in the target model's interface (see §2).
3. Paste the prompt into the input field **without modification**.
4. Submit the prompt.
5. Wait for the complete response to render.
6. Copy only the code block from the response. If the model produces
   both explanation text and a code block, only the code block is retained.
7. Save the code verbatim to a temporary file without any editing.
8. Repeat twice more (three runs total per model per task).

**No follow-up prompts, clarification requests, or re-submissions were issued.**
If a model produced non-runnable output (e.g., pseudo-code or explanatory prose
without a code block), that run was recorded as a failed run and included in the
three-run pool.

---

## 4. Run Selection

Three independent runs were conducted per model per task. The primary specimen
selected for metric measurement was the run achieving the **highest unit-test
pass rate** (as measured by the pre-written pytest suite).

**Tiebreaker:** In the event of a pass-rate tie across multiple runs, the output
from **Run 1** (the first session) was selected.

**Transparency note:** This best-of-3 selection protocol produces an **upper
bound** on model correctness performance rather than the expected average across
deployments. This is acknowledged as a limitation in `docs/limitations.md` and
in the paper's limitations section.

---

## 5. Model Version Recording

All three models were accessed on **2025-04-01**. Model versioning was
confirmed as follows:

| Model | Version Confirmation Method |
|---|---|
| ChatGPT | "GPT-4o" label in the model dropdown at session start |
| Claude | "Claude 3.5 Sonnet" label in the model selector |
| GitHub Copilot | Extension version v1.200.0 confirmed in VS Code Extensions panel |

**Important:** All three language model backends are proprietary and subject to
server-side updates. The model versions confirmed above reflect the state
accessible on 2025-04-01 and may not correspond identically to future or past
model states of the same version label. See `docs/limitations.md` §4.

---

## 6. Evaluation Order

To reduce order effects, metric measurements were performed in the following
fixed order for every (task, model) pair:

1. Unit tests (pytest) — executed first to assign primary specimen
2. pylint static analysis
3. radon Cyclomatic Complexity
4. timeit runtime measurement
5. Manual Big-O classification (both raters independently)
6. Manual readability rubric scoring (both raters independently)
7. Cohen's Kappa computation and disagreement resolution discussion

**Hardware:** All automated evaluations (steps 1–4) were performed on the
same physical machine:

- CPU: Intel Core i5-12400 (6 cores, 2.5 GHz base)
- RAM: 16 GB DDR4
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
- Python: 3.11.9 (system-managed venv, isolated per task)

---

## 7. Manual Assessment Procedure

### 7.1 Big-O Classification

Both raters independently analyzed the algorithmic structure of each code
sample and assigned a Big-O time complexity class. Classifications were
compared; any disagreement was resolved through structured discussion
referencing standard algorithm analysis references.

### 7.2 Readability Rubric

Both raters independently completed the scoring sheet in
`rubric/readability_rubric.md` for all 30 code samples before comparing
scores. Cohen's Kappa was computed per dimension and overall.

**Minimum acceptable inter-rater reliability:** κ ≥ 0.61 (substantial
agreement, per Cohen 1960). If κ fell below this threshold, the rubric
criterion was reviewed and disagreements re-adjudicated until agreement
was reached.

---

## 8. Data Storage and Version Control

All collected code samples were committed to the repository immediately
after collection, before any metric evaluation began. Git commit timestamps
serve as an independent record of data collection timing.

The repository is hosted at:
https://github.com/spzhrrr/Paper-RM-ai-code-quality-evaluation
